title: Bandwidth-Aware Mini-Batch Fallbacks and Typed Tool Contracts — PRD Sketch
body:
Context:
This is a working PRD sketch exploring a combined approach to: (1) making streaming calls robust under variable client bandwidth and small-message workloads, (2) providing a predictable mini-batch fallback path when low-bandwidth or high-concurrency conditions make continuous streaming inefficient, and (3) defining a lightweight typed tool contract that the SDK can use to exercise graceful degradation and deterministic reconciliation.

Why this problem now:
- Customers are building latency-sensitive UIs (search assistants, chat UIs, compositional tools) that rely on incremental tokens for perceived responsiveness.
- On mobile and low-bandwidth environments, continuous tiny-chunk streaming causes high per-request overhead (connection churn, per-frame transport costs) and increases our tail latency/cost.
- Existing streaming PRDs are focused on protocol and client ergonomics; we need an operationally inexpensive fallback that keeps UX fluid while controlling cost.

Goal (product-level):
Provide an API and SDK pattern that: 
- Keeps perceived latency low for end users on constrained networks.
- Reduces per-token cost by switching to short mini-batches when streaming is suboptimal.
- Exposes a typed tool-call contract for downstream integrations so tool invocations remain deterministic across streaming vs fallback modes.
- Surfaces telemetry to decide routing and to measure UX regressions.

Non-goals:
- Full overhaul of the streaming wire protocol (we will extend existing streaming frames instead).
- Strongly typed schema enforcement beyond simple typed envelopes: this is a pragmatic contract to enable safe parsing and replay.

Design sketch (high level):
1) Bandwidth/latency probe + local heuristics (client SDK)
- SDK runs a lightweight probe on connection open and periodically: RTT + effective throughput estimate based on small HTTP/HTTP2 frames or WebSocket pings.
- SDK exposes decision: STREAM (continuous chunking) vs MINI_BATCH (aggregate tokens for N ms or until M tokens).
- Default heuristic: if client throughput < 150 kbps or observed chunk drop/slow ack rate, prefer MINI_BATCH. Configurable via client options and server-side override via header X-RW-Stream-Mode.

2) Mini-batch fallback behavior
- In MINI_BATCH mode the SDK will buffer partial tokens up to a short time window (e.g., 150ms–600ms depending on latency budget) and send/receive multi-token frames similar to a small sync generation.
- Server runtime will process mini-batches with lower overhead than per-token streaming (reduced flushes, combined kernel runs).
- The streaming wire includes a frame type: STREAM_MODE=mini_batch and a sequence id for reconciliation.

3) Typed tool-call envelope (lightweight contract)
- Each tool invocation or final output chunk uses a typed envelope structure: { "kind": "text|tool_call|meta", "schema": "v1/simple-tool", "payload": "..." }.
- schema is a short string; we will publish a small set of canonical schemas (simple-tool, http-call, sql-query, file-op). Payload is JSON string in the envelope.
- For streaming, partial tool_call frames can include an incremental state token: {"incomplete": true, "cursor": "abc"}. When fallback to MINI_BATCH occurs, server assembles final payload and emits a completion frame with incomplete=false and same cursor.
- This design ensures idempotent reconstitution of tool calls in clients that expect typed outputs.

4) SDK ergonomics and API surface
- Primary surface: RedwoodClient.stream(...) and RedwoodClient.generate(...). We add optional param streamMode: "auto|prefer_stream|prefer_batch|force_stream|force_batch" and latencyBudgetMs.
- SDK returns an async iterator for stream mode and a promise for final generation for batch mode. For hybrid usage, the iterator yields partial typed envelopes; a final envelope with kind="complete" indicates completion.
- Convenience: RedwoodClient.streamHybrid(...) that accepts onPartial(envelope) and onToolCall(toolEnvelope) callbacks and provides .mode() introspection for debugging.
- Backpressure: provide client-level leaky-bucket write window; when the client cannot push, local SDK will automatically increase mini-batch window to avoid dropped frames.

API examples (sketch):
- Request header: X-RW-Stream-Mode: auto
- Partial streaming frame (server -> client): {"seq": 123, "frame": {"kind":"text","schema":"v1/plain","payload":"The ans"}}
- Mini-batch completion frame: {"seq":123,"frame":{"kind":"text","schema":"v1/plain","payload":"The answer is 42","complete":true}}
- Tool call begin (stream): {"seq":124,"frame":{"kind":"tool_call","schema":"simple-tool","payload":"{\"name\":\"google-search\",\"q\":\"redwood inference\"}","incomplete":true,"cursor":"c1"}}
- Tool call final (mini-batch completion): {"seq":124,"frame":{"kind":"tool_call","schema":"simple-tool","payload":"{\"name\":\"google-search\",\"q\":\"redwood inference\",\"result\":...}","incomplete":false,"cursor":"c1","complete":true}}

Acceptance criteria (v0):
- SDK can toggle between streaming and mini-batch modes via heuristic and explicit flag.
- Server emits typed frames (kind/schema) and maintains cursor-based reconciliation for tool calls.
- Latency: perceived first-token latency within 250ms for STREAM on good networks and within 400ms for MINI_BATCH on low-bandwidth simulated clients.
- Cost: server-side experiments show >=10% token compute reduction for low-bandwidth traffic by combining mini-batches versus naive per-token streaming.
- Telemetry: metrics exposed per-route: stream_mode_selected, average_mini_batch_window_ms, tool_call_reconciled_rate, partial_retransmits.

Rollout plan (experimental):
- Phase 0 (internal): SDK + runtime flags behind feature gate. Internal dogfooding in Redwood Console chat and tooling. Collect metrics 2 weeks.
- Phase 1 (opt-in customers): expose streamMode option to customers; run A/B comparing default auto vs force_stream on samples.
- Phase 2 (gradual default change): if mini-batch cost/latency tradeoffs are favorable for specific client regions (mobile APAC), flip default auto heuristic to be more mini-batch friendly.

Telemetry and measurement proposal:
- New lightweight counters/tags: stream_mode (stream|mini_batch), probe_bandwidth_kbps (binned), client_platform (mobile|desktop), avg_partial_size_chars, tool_call_cursor_reused (bool).
- Dashboards: percent traffic in mini-batch, conversions (UX metrics: user perceived time to first meaningful chunk), and cost delta per token.

Risks & mitigations:
- Risk: Inconsistent tool invocation semantics between streaming and mini-batch could produce duplicate tool calls.
  Mitigation: Server enforces idempotency via cursor and server-side dedupe; SDK replays only when final complete frame not seen.
- Risk: Increased complexity in SDKs (multiple platforms).
  Mitigation: Provide minimal idiomatic SDK layer; default behavior is automatic, only advanced users use hybrid APIs.
- Risk: Hard to tune mini-batch windows across all networks.
  Mitigation: Start with conservative windows and collect telemetry to drive per-region tuning.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Protocol: Do we piggyback mode preference in existing OPEN_STREAM frames or add dedicated header? (engineering input)
- Schema governance: Do we publish 'simple-tool' schemas in the public model catalog, or keep them internal for now? (policy/legal)
- Runtime: How does mini-batch scheduling interact with current dynamic batching kernel heuristics? Need bench tests on 8k/16k models. (scheduling/perf)

Implementation notes for eng teams (rough):
- Serving runtime: add a stream_mode flag to connection context, add a per-connection mini-batch buffer with flush policy; ensure KV cache pointers unaffected.
- SDKs: add probe and streamMode option, implement async iterator hybrid helper, ensure backpressure window and automatic window expansion logic.
- Console: add a stream_mode filter on recent calls, telemetry chart for mini-batch ratio and per-call cost.

Notes to self (brain dump):
- Experiment idea: use ML model in the edge SDK to predict chunk drop probability and tune mini-batch window adaptively. Too fancy for v0 but interesting.
- For A/B, measure both server cost and end-user satisfaction (session retention, perceived latency).
- Keep the typed envelope small – we don't want heavy schema negotiation in initial rollout.

Appendix: Example SDK usage (JS sketch)
const client = new RedwoodClient({apiKey: process.env.RW_KEY});
// automatic mode, low latency preference
for await (const frame of client.stream({prompt, streamMode: 'auto', latencyBudgetMs: 250})) {
  if (frame.kind === 'text') renderPartial(frame.payload);
  if (frame.kind === 'tool_call') executeToolPreview(frame.payload);
}

Summary:
This PRD sketch favors a pragmatic, operationally aware approach: keep streaming ergonomics for good networks while introducing a constrained mini-batch fallback that reduces cost and behaves deterministically through a small typed envelope for tool-calls. Next steps: align with serving runtime and SDK owners, run performance microbenchmarks, and prototype an opt-in SDK feature for dogfood testing.
